slides.title: Decision policy: input, scores, action
slides.notes: A learned policy is a mapping from state to action. We train it by supervised imitation, not RL. The provided utility rule expresses our toy objective.

items: 1,250 trainable parameters; no Transformer required.

slides.title: Define the decision objective before training
slides.notes: Accept only if it is affordable and profitable. Ties prefer wait. Model inference does not call this oracle; the rule supplies labels and evaluates regret.

slides.title: The complete learned decision architecture
slides.notes: Linear layers learn weights; ReLU supplies nonlinearity. The output is logits, not calibrated probability. Inputs are scaled by 9 outside the module.

slides.title: One supervised update
slides.notes: Both families use this update. D1 supplies action cross-entropy; the GPT supplies response-token cross-entropy. Finite checks and gradient clipping surface failures.

items: D1: cross_entropy(policy(features), oracle_actions).

slides.title: Decision evaluation includes utility
slides.notes: Accuracy can hide costly errors. Regret compares the chosen reward to the oracle's reward; it is not inferred from classification confidence.

items: Not a Decision Transformer, reinforcement learner, or real-world decision adviser.

slides.title: Reasoning is a training target, not a magic layer
slides.notes: Reuse the exact causal GPT implementation. Two blocks, width 64, four heads, context 32. Both models start from identical random weights; neither inherits Archive weights.

items: R0 and R1 each have 118,528 parameters.

slides.title: An explicit two-step program
slides.notes: The first running state is max(a,b); the second is min(that,c). Digits are visible program states, not hidden thoughts or natural-language rationalizations.

blocks.text:
def reasoning_example(values, scratchpad):
    validate_values(values)
    prompt = "cap(" + ",".join(map(str, values)) + ")="
    running, steps = values[0], []
    for index, value in enumerate(values[1:]):
        running = max(running, value) if index % 2 == 0 else min(running, value)
        steps.append(running)
    response = ",".join(map(str, steps if scratchpad else steps[-1:])) + "\n"
    return prompt, response

slides.title: Same problem, different supervised response
slides.notes: Answer-only and scratchpad learning are both supervised sequence prediction. R1 provides extra intermediate labels; R0 does not.

items: Step 1: max(8,2)=8. Step 2: min(8,5)=5.
Model-generated 9,5 has a correct answer but a wrong trace.

slides.title: Shifted response-only supervision
slides.notes: Ignored targets remove prompt and padding loss. The final prompt byte predicts the first response byte. Causal attention prevents later padding from affecting earlier outputs.

blocks.text:
def response_batch(cases, scratchpad):
    if not cases:
        raise ValueError("A supervised batch cannot be empty.")
    examples = [reasoning_example(case, scratchpad) for case in cases]
    length = max(len(encode(prompt + response)) - 1 for prompt, response in examples)
    x = torch.zeros((len(cases), length), dtype=torch.long)
    y = torch.full_like(x, -100)
    for row, (prompt, response) in enumerate(examples):
        tokens = encode(prompt + response)
        x[row, :len(tokens) - 1] = torch.tensor(tokens[:-1])
        # The final prompt token predicts the first response token.
        start = len(encode(prompt)) - 1
        y[row, start:start + len(encode(response))] = torch.tensor(encode(response))
    return x, y

slides.title: Teacher forcing is not free generation
slides.notes: During training the correct first step is in the input when predicting the final answer. At test time only the prefix is supplied; all response tokens are generated.

items: Training: correct previous response tokens; response-only loss.
Testing: greedy GPT.generate(top_k=1); stop scoring at first newline.
Verifier checks generated transitions, not teacher-forced predictions.
Malformed responses and missing steps count as failures.

slides.title: Disjoint cases and checkpoint selection
slides.notes: Entire triples are disjoint. One seed and a small finite relation are not evidence of general reasoning. R1 has longer responses, so update-matching is not compute-matching.

items: 800 training / 100 validation / 100 test triples; split seed 2026.
R0/R1: same initial weights, seed, sampled cases and 4,000 updates.
Select lowest validation loss every 200 updates; then open tests.
R0: 128 supervised bytes/batch. R1: 256 bytes/batch.

slides.title: Measured heldout outcomes: no invented advantage
slides.notes: R0 already solves this small task perfectly. R1 demonstrates inspectable intermediate computation, not higher final-answer accuracy on this test.

items: 100 unseen input triples; free generation, not teacher-forced accuracy.

slides.title: Longer computation exposes the boundary
slides.notes: Four operands require three alternating max/min states. R1 does not complete the required longer trace. Strict-format answer scoring counts incomplete traces as failures.

items: A learned two-step format does not automatically become a general executor.
